comments.author: @PhilipWong55
comments.text:
As technology becomes more widespread, all nations have the chance to achieve their maximum economic potential, irrespective of their population size. The extent of each country's growth will depend on how effectively each individual can contribute to the best of their capabilities, as well as how the benefits are shared equitably.

Scarcity is a fundamental economic problem that has shaped the development of many economic systems, including capitalism, socialism, and communism.

Imagine a world where the availability of goods and services is not limited by scarcity, but instead by abundance. Thanks to advanced automation and artificial intelligence, the production and distribution of goods and services can be fully automated and highly efficient.

In such a world, basic needs such as food, shelter, and healthcare would be abundant and accessible to all, without the need for people to work to earn a living. Instead, people could pursue their passions and interests, and contribute to society in ways that are meaningful to them.

The role of work would shift from being a means of survival to a means of personal fulfillment and creativity. Education and personal growth would be valued for their own sake, rather than as a means of acquiring skills for employment.

Diversity is important for the survival of a human system because it provides resilience and adaptability. Without diversity, a system becomes more vulnerable to systemic failure and unable to respond to changing circumstances.

Things will keep changing; hopefully, they will always be for the better.

comments.author: @NikoKun
comments.text:
The only evidence economists point to, when they claim "new jobs will be created", are the jobs that didn't exist in 1940? Are they simple-in-the-head or something, or just looking for an easy excuse to wave the AI job displacement concern away? Cause merely looking at history, in this case, isn't very reassuring. What possible "new jobs" won't also be able to be automated? Or to put it another way, we're talking about the automation of cognitive tasks, by automated AI agents that will soon be as smart as, if not more so, than the average worker. So ask yourself, how will average workers compete against AI smarter than them, and much faster? The supposed "new jobs" would have to be tasks that couldn't be automated by AI, and I just don't see those sorta jobs magically appearing out of no where.
What they're likely referring to, is that there'll still be plenty of "things" for people to do.. It's just whether those things are capable of generating enough value to earn a survivable income, is likely going to be an issue. So we need to find ways to ensure everyone has the means to do things that are productive in their community, without necessarily requiring them to survive doing it. We really do need a UBI, as some form of AI Dividend.

comments.author: @dianes6245
comments.text:
AI has already hit its limit.  It wont get any better. Its limit is the 2048 token limit, and that wont budge because of a little known idea. Factorial math. It kills AI. Smashes it dead. No where else will you see this idea. But its OCO. Obvious to the most casual observer.  Now...if LLMs stay at this level, they will be used. And the ability to use them well will increase. but that comes at a cost. Human labor.  It will cost you money to use an LLM. Later you will get benefits, for sure. An LLM must be under the supervison of a human constantly. You got to baby sit your kid.  

Think airplane.  Passenger jets got big and fast in 1950. But not much has changed. 

Intelligence is the ability to compare things in complex ways. Its not about magic computations. Comparisons are factorial. Bad.  Its Real bad!  It blows out exponential growth, like a cheetah to an earthworm. Try it yourself. 5! vs e^5, then 10! vs e^10 and keep going. Its a hard wall that likely manifests itself in the 2048 token limit.  You cant do much with 2048. 

So... there aint gonna be any big AGI.  Nvidia and its huge growth is moot, because its the little earthworm in the factorial problem, despite its apparent "explosion".
